## 📜 What *is* Public Domain Poetry?

Public domain poems can be used, shared, and reproduced without permission because the copyright has expired (typically 70 years after the author’s death in the UK).

Most British poems in the public domain are by authors who died before 1955 (e.g., Victorian, Georgian, and early 20th-century writers).

## ❗ About *Newest* British Public Domain Poetry

Currently, *very recent British poetry* (e.g., works published after mid-20th century or by poets who died less than 70 years ago) is **not yet in the public domain** in the UK.

For example:

- Modern British poets like **Simon Armitage** (alive) or **Carol Ann Duffy** (died 2024) are *not* in the public domain (Duffy’s works will enter public domain 70 years post-death). citeturn0search45

## **Thomas Traherne — “Wonder”**
~~~{ "variant":"standard", "id":"48321" }
How like an Angel came I down!
How bright are all things here!
When first among His Works I did appear
O how their Glory did me crown!
The World resembled His Eternity,
In which my Soul did Walk;
And every Thing that I did see
Did with me talk.

The Skies in their Magnificence,
The lovely, lively Air,
O how divine, how soft, how fair!
The Stars did entertain my Sense;
And all the Works of God so bright
And glorious were,
As if they ever must endure
In my Esteem so great and fair.

Eternity was manifest
In Light and Life and Joy,
Revealing all Things that are best,
And free from all Alloy.

I felt no Sin nor Shame, no Fear nor Care;
The World was mine, and Heaven too;
No creature that did know
Was ever yet so rich as I.
~~~

---

## **Thomas Traherne — “The Salutation”**
~~~{ "variant":"standard", "id":"48322" }
These little Limbs,
These Eyes and Hands which here I find,
This panting Heart, this breathing Mind,
Were born to serve.

This World, my Joy,
This shining Sphere,
This glorious Sphere of Earth and Air,
Is God’s own Gift.

The Sun and Stars
That crown the Skies,
The moving Seas, the flowery Meads,
The Rivers and the Trees,
Are mine.

All Things are mine;
Whether the Sun doth shine,
Or Rain doth fall,
Or Night doth close,
Or Day doth rise,
Or Worlds their various Courses take,
Or Suns do set or rise,
All Things are mine.

The Winds and Rains,
The Frost and Snow,
The Floods and Storms,
The Clouds and Fire,
The Earth and Air,
The Sun and Sky,
The Sea and Land,
Are mine.

The End for which all these were made
Is mine;
The Love of God, the Breath of Life,
The Joys of Heaven,
Are mine.

The Person that was born
The Soul that was created,
The Mind that thought,
The Will that chose,
The Love that moved,
Are mine.

O sacred Joy!
O heavenly Bliss!
O wonderful Delight!
My World, my All,
My God, my King,
My Portion and my Crown.
~~~

Yes — that reaction makes complete sense.

**That’s exactly why *The Salutation* feels so striking today.**  
It comes from a mental world that is almost **absent** in a culture surrounded by accumulation, ownership, leverage, branding, optimisation.

Traherne isn’t saying *“I want”* or *“I take”*.  
He’s saying:

- *Everything already is*  
- *Nothing needs to be seized*  
- *Value precedes possession*

What feels unfamiliar now:

- **No competition** — nothing is scarce in the poem  
- **No anxiety** — no fear of missing out, no comparison  
- **No extraction** — the world is received, not exploited  
- **No performance** — joy exists without being displayed or monetised  

Even the repeated **“Are mine”** isn’t greedy.  
It’s almost the *opposite* of modern ownership.

Today, “mine” usually means:
- exclusion
- control
- advantage

For Traherne, “mine” means:
- participation
- belonging
- gratitude

That mindset is rare now — not because it’s naïve, but because it **doesn’t fit systems built on scarcity and pressure**.

So when you say it feels *interesting but unfamiliar*, that’s not distance —  
that’s recognition of something **we’ve lost touch with**.

If you want, we can:
- stay quietly with *why* this clashes with modern greed,
- or trace how this way of seeing slowly disappeared,
- or contrast it with a modern poem that feels hollow by comparison.

Just tell me which direction feels right.
